title: The first sign (John 2:1–11)
hookLine: John calls miracles signs: they point past themselves

lines: A ROAD SIGN ISN'T THE CITY.
cards: A road sign that says Chicago, 40 miles is not Chicago. Nobody pulls over and takes a selfie with it as if they've arrived. Its whole job is to point somewhere else.
Today's word is sign, the word John chooses, again and again, for what the Douay-Rheims calls miracles.
And the first one happens somewhere you wouldn't expect: not in the temple, not at a sickbed, but at a village wedding in Cana of Galilee, on the third day, when the wine runs out.

teach.b: Mary is the one who speaks up: "They have no wine." Just that. His answer sounds cool to our ears: woman, what is that to me and to thee? my hour is not yet come.
Woman is the same word he will use for her from the cross, and Mary seems to hear something other than no.

teach.h: WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY, DO YE.
teach.b: She tells the servants: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." They're her last recorded words in John's Gospel.

teach.h: SIX JARS, FILLED TO THE BRIM.
teach.b: There are six stone water jars, used for the Jewish rites of washing, each holding two or three measures. Fill them with water, he says, and they fill them to the brim. Draw some out, and take it to the steward.

The steward tastes it, has no idea where it came from, and calls the bridegroom over: everyone serves the good wine first, and the poorer wine once the guests have drunk well, "But thou hast kept the good wine until now."

John closes it this way: "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee; and manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him." Where the Douay says miracles, John's Greek says signs, semeia.

teach.h: NOT A MIRACLE ONLY, A SIGN.
teach.b: A sign isn't the destination. It points to who he is.
Here, water for washing becomes wine for a feast.
Saint John Paul the Second made Cana one of the Luminous Mysteries of the rosary, so those who pray the rosary come back to this wedding, and to Mary's words to the servants.

how: Catholics pray the Wedding at Cana as the second of the Luminous Mysteries of the rosary, usually on Thursdays, and often take Mary's words to the servants as a short summary of her role.

o: a trick performed to win over a crowd
a deed that points past itself to who he is
a warning from heaven that judgment is near

p: filled six stone jars to the brim
thou hast kept the good wine until now

s: John's Gospel calls Jesus's miracles signs
semeia: deeds that point past themselves to who he is.
Jesus refused, and Mary had to drop it
after his answer she tells the servants: whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye. and he acts.
the water came from a well and was poured into wineskins
it was six stone jars for the Jewish washing rites, filled to the brim.

games.q: you're Mary at a wedding. the wine has run out at the feast. your son has just said his hour is not yet come. what do you do?
o: drop it and say nothing more.
tell the servants: do whatever he tells you.
games.why: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." the water becomes wine, and the steward says the good wine was kept until now.

practice: Go back over today slowly, like flipping through photos on your phone, and look for one small thing that pointed past itself: a kindness out of nowhere, a meal that tasted better than it should, a moment that felt like more than it was.
Don't force it into anything big; just notice where it pointed. If you pray, thank God for it; if you don't, let it be a sign of something good.

wordCard.voice: Sign. John's word for Jesus's miracles, semeion in Greek: a deed that points past itself to who he is. The first was at Cana. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a sign, a mark that points beyond itself. John's word for Jesus's miracles.

carryVoice: Your line: the good wine until now. The best, kept for last. Day four hundred ninety-six, done.
